571.t: Her 101-year-old grandmother and a few Senegalese words
571.s: Alice remembers her grandmother, who died in 1910 aged 101, and the African words she taught her, such as 'Salicum Serum' for good morning.
571.q: If I remember my grandmother, oh Lord, yes. If I remember my grandmother. Seems like she's right in front of me now. And I miss her. I miss her. She was 101 years and 15 days when she died.

571.t: Learning English, thinking in French and speaking Creole to George
571.s: Alice says her grandmother spoke no English, her mother Creole and French, and she herself preferred French, falling back on it when angry with George.
571.ch: Alice Zeno: languages and the King household
571.q: But sometimes, some things I can't bring out in English. And when I get to fussing with him and he make me mad, I take my French. French. And he just looks at me and laughs. He ought to speak French. Because I spoke French to him all his babyhood. My Sydney, my nephew that I raised from the age of…

571.t: French and Creole songs, including a Haitian revolution song
571.s: Alice tries to recall old songs and recites a Creole song about the Haitian revolution and hunger.
571.q: Uh-huh. Yes, I believe it is, because I'll tell you, the French song that I know is mostly mixed up. Uh-huh. Toe tae is siens, dee puis plus dee en zan, tapez, we'll tapez, we'll that's Creole. Uh-huh. Tapez soufer de la plus grande misère, mangez tes chers, pas tes gagnants l'argent, that's…

571.t: De De Pierce and the origin of Eh La Bas
571.s: Lewis was around when De De made up the tune, but cannot date it. Older people say it predates De De, though the jazz version is his.
571.ch: Day jobs and later Billy and De De engagements
571.q: No, I really don't know because so many people claim it, but from the older people I hear, it's been around before Dee Dee's time.

571.t: Children's ring games and songs: Les Ognons, Twinkle Twinkle
571.s: Alice sings 'Les Ognons' used in ring games, and the interviewers ask about Creole songs and songs at weddings.
571.q: Sometimes, sometimes... When I see George look down, you know, then... If something come, then I begin to sing it. Cheer him up.

571.t: Learning French as a child with the Mazzaro family
571.s: Alice was raised among the Mazzaro family who spoke only French to her for four or five years.
571.ch: Alice Zeno: languages and the King household
571.q: Well, French, I learned the French, you see, with the people my mother, when I was born, my mother was working, and as soon as she could go back on the job, she took me and the Miss Mazzaro. They had me in the house like a child, a white child. They didn't want my mother to have anything to do with…

571.t: Working as a maid for Mrs. King's family and the Miller relatives
571.s: Alice explains how she learned German and Spanish at the King household on Rampart, where she was housegirl for Nina King, and names the family's relatives.
571.ch: Alice Zeno: languages and the King household
571.q: Oh, yes. They had Mrs. TJ Samms cross the street, Mrs. McCall, Mrs. Morris. But all them people moved, you know, uptown because the neighborhood had gotten to be so bad.

571.t: Language classes at the King house and Miss Gracie's advice
571.s: Alice describes the daily French, Spanish and German conversation classes in the household and how she learned to take the opportunity seriously.
571.ch: Alice Zeno: languages and the King household
571.q: In French. In French. Well, you see, when I was working at Mrs. King, they had...it wasn't a school. It was just like you're nice, convoicing you. Yes. They had Mr. Chaffray. You must have heard of that name, Chaffray? I'm not sure.

868.t: Creole word list: furniture, body, nature and everyday words
868.s: Pearsall takes De De through words for objects, body parts, verbs and animals, each repeated three times for the recording.
868.q: let me see how can you use the light together you say light on it illuminé say it again illuminé again illuminé illuminé

868.t: How De De learned French and Creole; the Creole jargon
868.s: De De says his mother learned French at the convent and he learned Creole and a broken-up jargon from his family; it is now spoken by few.
868.q: Right through my people. They're talking to me in and out, French and the Creole, sometimes mixed, you know. That's how that came about.

868.t: More words and phrases: going to town, rain, sun, hot
868.s: Pearsall and Allen ask for further Creole words and sentences such as 'I am going to town' and 'it is going to rain'.
868.q: Parler. Parler. Parler. Parler. Parler. En ville. En ville. En ville. En ville. And what's that mean? Upkeep. And what's that mean? Uptown, like in town.

868.t: Lyrics of 'A La Ba', first verse: the hog and hot sausage
868.s: De De translates the opening verse word by word: going to market for a hog, none to be had, hot sausage instead.
868.q: The other day, La-Jur. Again? La-Jur means the other day. Yeah, oh the other day. The other day. The other day. And what is today? Jardie. And the other day again, I want to get that one more time. La-Jur.

868.t: 'A La Ba' verse: my dear cousin and your kitchen
868.s: De De gives and explains a verse about eating well and drinking wine for free at a cousin's kitchen, and says he sometimes makes up verses as he sings.
868.q: Mon chère cousin, mon chère cousine, mon la main to la cuisine. Mon manger bien, mon bar plein de vin. Ça pas coûte moi rien. In other words, my dear cousin, my dear cousin, I love your kitchen. I eat good. I drink plenty wine. And it doesn't cost me anything.

868.t: Creole verbs and times of day: sleep, get up, French, morning
868.s: Allen asks for verbs and words like couche, arrive, Francais, Creole and matin.
868.q: See you. See you. See you. See you. My time this morning. Love you all yesterday. You're on the lead today.

868.t: Verse about the red fish cobayon, and the rice cake calla
868.s: De De translates a verse about his mother saying the stewed fish was not good for him, then explains calla, a rice cake.
868.q: I mean cobayon. Yeah cobayon cobayon. Poisson poisson poisson fish. Te right again. Te pabon was not good. Pabon pabon pabon. I mean not good not good. Po moin. Po moin for me for me for me. Po moin po moin po moin.

269.t: The Haitian revolution song learned from her grandmother
269.s: She sings a song of Haiti/Santo Domingo about the end of suffering and says she learned songs from her grandmother and mother.
269.q: Tout Haïtien depuis plus de onze ans T'a fait souffert de la plus grande misère Manger tes chers, pas tes gagner l'argent La fin t'es tuée déjà beaucoup de mer En bas, sal bas, enfin bénissant le Seigneur Y'a fait partir fausser par l'ordre de Renard Bon Dieu dans ciel pour finir l'injustice De ces…

269.t: Her Senegalese great-grandmother and the songs she passed down
269.s: Her great-grandmother was brought from Senegal at eight, remembered her father's name, and sang songs for the children; Paraco translated the language.
269.q: Senegal See, with Senegalian That's how we knew so many of them songs, you see And just now, because I want to remember my kids

269.s: Her grandmother spoke Senegalese to her alone and taught her expressions and greetings, though few songs.
269.q: No. But she speak to me. I was only one she speak her language too. Because my mother didn't want to go talk that with Alice. Don't come to me with that. Go talk that with Alice. And I loved it. I followed every step she made. And I'd ask her. Again, show me. Tell me. Yes, tell me.

269.s: Pepe-pate, red beans with bananas, tum tum and gumbo; Zeno misses her grandmother.
269.q: I didn't like it much on account of that pepe-pate, that black pepper, you know? Yes. And she used to make funny dishes, you know, her home dish.

269.t: Languages at the King household and the Ranshaw family
269.s: Working for Mrs. King she picked up Spanish and French from teachers who gave classes; she talks about Gladys Ranshaw and the judge she served.
269.ch: Working for the King and Ranshaw families
269.q: Well, it's the language that I could read with more facilité, you know. Yes. But I read because, you see, old Mrs. W. W. King, Grace King. Her mother? Huh? Grace King's mother? Grace King's mother. I worked there. And there they used to have classes every three, about four days in the week. One day…

1.t: French, Creole and Cajun spoken around his childhood
1.s: His grandparents spoke French and Creole, which Barker heard but was not encouraged to speak.
1.q: My grandmother spoke French. My grandfather spoke French. They also spoke Creole, that is, a broken French. In the country they had another French, was called Cajun [Barker pronouces it “ki-jeune.”] Different varieties of French. There was, say, bread in different . . . about five different ways of…

1.t: The she-brick that spits on you
1.s: Danny explains a loose paving brick that squirts water, and his grandfather's skill in avoiding it.
1.ch: Wagon bands, halls and the old brass bands
1.q: You'd see little kids, you know, who were just fascinated by what they were playing in the street. And you would have to watch for a (?) stone or a she-brick. Now, what you call a she-brick is when it rains. See, in a loose brick, the water is under this brick...

1.t: Longhead Bob's string band and Creole songs
1.s: Longhead Bob led a string group playing Creole songs and blues with improvised lyrics about love and food.
1.ch: Boyhood scene: halls and dance music
1.q: Longhead Bob had somewhat of a string group, played guitar. He had a string group and sometimes he'd argument a couple of brass men in his group. Most of it was a string group. And they played a lot of Creole songs, blues. I didn't know whether it was Catholic or Baptist because they jazzed up…

1.s: Danny describes his maternal grandparents Isadore Barbarin and Josephine and a Haitian great-grandmother who spoke French, Creole, Patois and Cajun.
1.ch: Childhood, family and the sounds of New Orleans
1.q: My mother's father's name was Isadore John Barbarin. His wife, his maiden name was Josephine Auphidore(?). Her grandmother's mother had came from Haiti. She spoke French, she spoke Creole, she spoke Patois and Cajol(?). All of them is different versions of the French, all of them spoke by different…

175.t: Creole language and Rena's number 'Eh La Bas'
175.s: His parents spoke Creole; Rena sang 'Eh La Bas' nightly, improvising words, and others also sang it.
175.ch: Kid Rena, Kelly and the old trumpeters
175.q: Yes, they learned French, I guess it was handed down to them from their mothers and fathers. But I guess maybe one of the reasons why I didn't learn too much about it, because I was probably out in the streets someplace trying to see what's going on. And the only thing about it, I noticed when they…

402.t: Claire singing; Broadwater Beach and Edgewater
402.s: Light talk about Claire's singing and the Gulf Coast hotels.
402.q: One night we had a band boy and she was singing up there. Brought the house down and we played somewhere. Why haven't we played? Joe Brown's place in Bulldogs in there.

904.t: Origin of Eh La Ba and the band becoming the Paul Barnes Band
904.s: Paul explains where Eh La Ba came from, D.D. Pierce's version, then the band takes his name and plays New Orleans.
904.q: D.D. Well, I'll tell you the facts of the thing. There's nobody around New Orleans wrote that. The, the, the, as far as I can, the man who composed it, I don't know his name, but he used to call him the Mayor of Pompon. That's all he said, he was the Mayor of Pompon. Yeah. And he used to sing that…

248.t: His parents' languages and a trip to Belize
248.s: His mother spoke French and his father, William Dawson, a ship worker from British Honduras, Spanish; the family visited Belize for a month but left because of mosquitoes.
248.ch: Early life and the Whitney Bank
248.q: No. My mama speaks French. My ma, my mother spoke French but I couldn't. My father, my father spoke Spanish. I was, I, I never did speak Mandeville, you know. Yeah. I could understand a little of it, you know. What was your father's name? William, William Dawson. William Dawson, I see. He run on a…

430.t: Creole songs and French spoken in the family
430.s: They recall Creole songs and say his parents and grandmother spoke only French at home.
430.q: Just a few words, I mean, he used to say most of them, he'd say, ay ay ay ay, mu pala meh sa, mu pala meh sa, mu pala meh sa.

955.s: The family spoke Creole, which was looked down on as broken French; stepfather sang in it.
955.q: Practically, we all grew up in Creole. Which they didn't want you to learn that, because they called it, said it was a broken French. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. And just grew up with it. Did anybody around your house sing songs in Creole? Or? Well, my daddy used to, my stepfather. Mm-hmm .

724.t: Creole French at home, a lesson teacher and a home recording
724.s: His mother spoke French; he sings Creole songs; he had a few lessons and a home recording with Giles.
724.q: Oh, what about Elah Bar? That's always been one of these special numbers. How long you been playing that? Oh, since I stopped playing. Well, I know you know plenty of those Creole words and all that. Did your family speak French in the home? Yeah. My mother would speak to us in French and we'd…

255.t: Repertoire of the family band and Creole songs
255.s: The family played jigs, self-made songs and many Creole songs, including the first singer of 'A La Ba'.
255.q: Falses or what? Well, they had all kind of different numbers like jigs and so forth like that. You know, it wasn't as fast as it is now, you know? Then they'd have a lot of numbers that they'd make up their self. But I used to get an old man make up song, just with words. He'd make up his own…

646.t: No French or Creole where she lived
646.s: She says everyone was American with no French or Creole speakers, though the man knows Creole people.

752.t: Creole words and language in the Foster family
752.s: Talk about Creole words like coquette and Pops's mother's languages.

641.t: Growing up hearing French and Creole; the French-speaking dog and mules
641.s: His father spoke Creole and French; the children mostly listened, and he tells of a dog and farm animals that understood only French.
641.q: Did they speak French or Creole in the family? Oh, he, my father talked real French. He talked both, Creole and French. And probably English much less, huh? That's right.

252.t: Carrie Boote remembers the 1878 yellow fever epidemic
252.s: Carrie recalls the silent town, no bells, and playmates dying of yellow fever.
252.q: Well, I said that the... That was in May when... Well, all that I can say, I remember that time and date, you know, in 1878, when the yellow people were so bad that the trains wasn't... The bells wasn't ringing on the steam cars and the town was all quiet. No bells or whatsoever. The people were…

710.s: Bailey calls himself Creole but speaks only a little, such as bonsoir.
710.q: No, I never used to say. I'm Creole, but I never used to talk. Just a few little boys. Bonsoir. Bonsoir, and what else you say? Well, like Bonsoir. I didn't know something about it.

626.t: Creole language and the Creole people of Mobile
626.s: He talks about older Creoles speaking French, the broken French of Mon Louis Island, and his mother's and wife's French families.
626.ch: Church, Creole life and Mobile musicians
626.q: Well, some of them did, yeah. The older heads did. But, and coming up in the late days, they didn't take much interest in teaching their children. Did they have any special Creole songs in Creole? Do you remember? Down in Mononville Island they speak it, yeah. They call it the Broken French down…

297.t: Gaspard's multi-instrument skill, brother Octave and Creole speech
297.s: Gaspard played several horns; his brother Octave played bass; he spoke English with a Creole accent.
297.q: He was a great trombone player. Baritone, bass violin, bass horn. He played all that. Well, his brother was there. His brother played bass too, didn't he? Oh, yeah. Octave or something. Octave or something. Octave. They called him oak, I guess. Octave, yeah. Octave, yeah.

251.t: Grandfather's Dominican roots and descent from Dominique You
251.s: Albert traces the Dominique name to the Dominican Republic and a pirate ancestor, discusses why elders avoid family history, and mentions the ancestor's grave.
251.q: From what we understand and what we know from the Dominican Republic, derived the name Dominic Cutter-Hugh off of it. And I understand that his grandfather was Dominic Hugh, the pirate on the gene defense ship. Which is all authentic, because there's a lady died here just a few years ago. That was…

11.t: Papa Tio's reputation and home; Creole speech
11.s: Tio was only a teacher, charged whether you came or not, lived in the Creole section; Clem's French-speaking father.
11.q: Yeah, well, I didn't know him to play when I got acquainted with him and started. That's all he was doing, teaching. Yeah. And you'd have to pay him whether you come or not. He had that system.

873.t: Creole and French in Reserve, and English at school
873.s: Lawrence grew up speaking Creole; English came with school, and his children and grandchildren no longer understand it.
873.q: All of them. In this section. You couldn't find a not true family that was reading on here that could speak anything but Creole and French, you know. Some would speak French. What it comes. Some would speak French and most of them would speak Creole.

461.t: Religion and the Bowman and Rene families
461.s: Raised Catholic; describes his German grandfather Bowman, a shipping commissioner, and his father's French-descended family.
461.q: The old Catholic, I was raised a Catholic, and that's the time when the Catholic, I never forget my mother and father at that time, my grandfather was named Bowman, he was shipping commissioner here, what I meant, he had his charge of all the boats that came in from South America, those fruit boats…

151.t: Creole language and Reason's family background
151.s: Asked about French and Creole, Reason says his mother's family was Creole and gives her maiden name.
151.q: No. A little bit I did know when I got to King Alvarez's band, he said, forget it. He said, you come here with that band. He said, these boys be mad in this band. Yeah. He said, most of those fellas, they were from up north. Yeah. New York, you mean. And they always thought you was talking about…

799.t: French heritage and French songs in Louisiana
799.s: He is entirely French, fifth or sixth generation; his mother sang French songs, and he explains three French dialects in Louisiana.
799.q: Oh yeah, my mother used to sing quite a few of them. I think I just about forgot most of them, you know, little ditties and French folk songs, you know.

706.t: Africa and New Orleans: African ties and Swahili words
706.s: Asked if he thinks of himself as African, he recalls Africans in New Orleans and Swahili words like mumbo-jumbo and drum effects.
706.q: Yes, I have it in me, man. My great grandparents when I was a kid, I mean, and I met so many Africans in the weather and everything when I was in New Orleans as a child. There have always been Africans all over New Orleans.

629.t: Old Creole songs, his brother, and Mardi Gras
629.s: Picou says his brother composed Creole songs; they discuss titles and translations and playing them at Mardi Gras.
629.q: If my brother was living, and would be sitting right here now, he's the one that composed all Creole songs. Really? El Abado. What was his name? Eulis. Eulis. Eulis.

713.t: The song 'A La Ba' and the Creole language
713.s: Nelson first heard 'A La Ba' sung by Billy and Dee Dee; Burbank recorded it; Nelson knows no Creole despite coming from St. Bernard.
713.q: yeah Burbank but I was the first one I heard it and I was a small young fella it was Billy and Dee Dee

836.t: The tea, soiree and block dance cycle; patio and speakers
836.s: The year's events and photographs of a tea with a speaker reciting in French and the patio before the freeze.
836.ch: Photographs of the Creole Fiesta and family
836.q: And so we're always having something. Now, this is our tea. And we had...this lady was saying a speech for us. Now, this is my patio, the way it was with all...see all the leaves and everything? Now you can see what it looked like before the freeze. Now you can see what it looked like now.

665.t: Chairing the Tulane Club banquet committee
665.s: She loved cooking and was kept as chairman of the banquet committee.
665.q: Well, when I had the Tulane. Where is that book? I had Tulane Club. I went to California. I was appointed chairman of the club for a banquet. It's right in there. It is. I put it back on top. They just raise up your baby basket. And I said, well, I'm going to California. I ain't going to tell them…

282.t: Jim Robinson as his uncle and the Deer Range settlements
282.s: Jim Robinson is his mother's brother; Brown describes where families lived and the nearby places Junior and Woodland.
282.q: Oh, yeah, well, Jim is my uncle. He's my mother's brother. And, uh, well, we would live just about, he would be his, with his sister down that way, his mother was dead, see. And up this way further would be my house.

150.t: Creole identity today and African dress
150.s: Tex closes on writers like Lyle Saxon, who calls himself Creole today, and changing black fashion.
150.q: like I'm saying to each his own but this Creole thing we will always have people like Lyle Saxon and all these other writers of note who will write about them and talk about them but like I said it all depends on who they're talking about what era of time what went on back in the 1840s 1830s and so…

193.t: Learning the Creole song Hey La Ba
193.s: He says he learned the song from Creole-speaking elders and added words, not from a band.
193.q: Well, the pastor and I, of course, most of the men spoke Creole. Father Tim said, Hey, La, Ba. Hey, La, Ba. And just wanted to know a thing. Thought about it. And got up and sang. Put adding words, adding words to it. That's how I got started.

290.s: He played for Irish, calls himself Creole but cannot speak it, and discusses Creole singers.
290.q: Yeah, they had plenty of them. Well, I would say yes, if I didn't see one, because I know that was the place they supposed to be living. Yeah. Irish people were supposed to be living out there, so I would think they had plenty of them. Did you ever play at the Santa Center Club? Santa Center Club?…

52.t: Mobile song, Calypso in Nassau and a planned trip home
52.s: Mason links Mobile to a sailors' song heard in Nassau, describes Calypso and the bonefish song, and discusses his last visit to Miami and his planned return to Nassau.
52.q: Then, let's see, Baton Rouge and Donisonville, but never, never in a, never played in Mobile. I remember about Mobile, I was always, always intrigued about Mobile because when I was a boy down in Nassau, I'd go down to the wharf, down to the wharf when the ship's coming, I had a sailor sing a song,…

270.t: The big storm, his grandfather, and his great-aunt who read French
270.s: He recalls his grandfather's account of storm damage in New Orleans, relatives living in the city, and his French-reading seamstress great-aunt.
270.q: No, that big storm, I remember my grandfather was living. And I don't know whether he was here, but he had came to New Orleans after the storm. And he had... You know, my grandfather never did like New Orleans. I don't know why. And he had went down to the... I remember he was describing to the…

304.s: Wood recalls hardly any street cries and only a French-speaking family at Morrison's Cafeteria.
304.ch: Traditional style, ragtime orchestra and closing questions
304.q: I guess I do remember maybe somebody coming through selling strawberries uptown in the strawberry season. But, you know, it was an unusual thing. They were not a part of the scene when I was here in the 50s, at least of the scene that I was aware of.

537.t: Brunious family, Creole divisions and origin of the name
537.s: Relation to George Brunious and other Brunious musicians, passing for white Creoles, and the French origin of the name from Pau.
537.q: Yes. George Brunious, Mary Brunious and Abby Brunious and those guys, they were kin to my grandfather but coming from like a Creole family, things were so divided. You know whoever could, we had what we call pasa blanc Creoles, which means we’re white Creoles and there was so much opportunity on…

226.t: Origin of the Levy name on a Plaquemines Parish plantation
226.s: The name came from his paternal grandfather's enslaved family owned by French Jews in Plaquemines Parish.
226.q: Levy, as far as I could discern – the periods that I traced it was through my father’s father, who was part of a slave thing. All of the people on the plantation had the name of Levy. In other words, all of the slaves had the name of Levy. So that’s where the name came from.

427.t: Mistaken for a Creole in Louisiana
427.s: Patrons took him for Creole and spoke French; he insisted he was from Kansas City and his mother looked white.
427.ch: Washington, New Orleans and the road
427.q: So I...I say, "I wanna see some Creoles." "There's one, there's one, there's one, there's one, there's one." "Appear to me them's half-white folks. 'At's all they are."

30.t: French spoken at home and his grandmother's French books
30.s: He speaks some French, his family spoke only French and attended an all-French school, and he shows his grandmother's old French books.
30.q: No, only what I want to speak when I go in them different countries and when I want something or get some guy to tell me what I'd like, to go to a restaurant or a taxi, take him in a taxi till I get the layout of how much money I should give him, you know, whatever -- pesos or whatever. And things…

413.s: Hinton recalls his grandmother's Creole French.
413.ch: Learning from players; Jonah Jones lessons

455.s: Budd describes El Saieh's Arab and Lebanese family background, the family business and his art dealing.
455.ch: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
455.q: His father was Arabic. And his mother was from Bethlehem. So she was Lebanese, and she was born -- she told me when I was down there -- her house was right across from the manger where Jesus Christ was born, and of course they have a place where they have a business called the Haitian and American…
